messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Threat
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Ethan, a 29‑year‑old North American male, has spent the past six years working as a jeweler in a small shop in Seattle. In 2017, while volunteering with a relief organization in the war‑torn city of Aleppo, he witnessed the sudden collapse of a building that had housed children’s hospital supplies. A fragment of the wall burst, a shard of glass sliced his hand, and a distant explosion tore the air. He remembered the scream of a little boy, the crunch of broken glass, and the sudden, unblinking eye of a soldier holding a rifle that flicked as the building shuddered. That day, his heart leapt, and he felt the ground vibrate beneath his feet. The memory of that moment is what still haunts him. In the months after he returned home, ordinary sounds, sights, and even touches would trigger an onslaught of sensations. The rapid beating of his heart would catch him in the middle of a conversation about diamonds, and a child’s cry from a nearby playground would make his stomach drop as if he were again in a war zone. A stranger’s unexpected touch on his arm during a jewelry appraisal would send a shiver through his spine. When these triggers surfaced, he would feel as though a flood of fear rushed in from the past. He would think, “It could have been worse,” and force his mind to keep a positive narrative in place, trying to convince himself that all the good he had done in Aleppo mattered. He would scan his surroundings, looking for hidden threats, pausing before he could take a deep breath. He was certain that he could only feel safe when his back was against a wall and he could see the entire room; even when his shopkeeper told him that the shop was secure, he could not believe that safety was guaranteed. When Ethan hears children crying, the sound instantly floods him with the memory of the battle, the memory compels him to reassure himself that it could have been worse, the memory causes him to keep his mind in constant positive thought, the memory forces him to check the shop for hidden weapons, the memory makes him feel unsafe, the memory keeps him scanning, the memory keeps him feeling that the shop is dangerous. When he feels his heart racing, he thinks that it could have been worse, he scans, he feels that it could be dangerous, he forces positive thoughts, he remembers a time when a child cried and a gunshot rang in his mind, he feels unsafe because he cannot trust that the shop is safe, he looks for weapons, and he keeps his back against the wall. When a stranger touches him, he immediately thinks it could have been worse, he scans, he forces positivity, he remembers the wall fragment, he feels unsafe, he keeps his back against the wall, he sees the threat, and he thinks he cannot trust safety. These loops tighten the more he lives with them. Every time a child’s cry ricochets from a nearby street, his heart starts pounding as if the battle were happening again. The flash of that memory is not accompanied by a clear image; instead, he feels the emotional intensity as if it were a fresh injury, and the recall feels more real than any ordinary memory. Each time this occurs, he engages in his maladaptive strategies, which then feed back into his perception of threat and memory, creating a vicious cycle that he cannot escape. In his shop, this manifests as avoidance of certain clients who ask him to handle precious gems with close contact. He has stopped using gloves for fear of being touched unexpectedly, and he refuses to let anyone touch a ring he has cleaned. The shop’s lighting is dimmed so that he can keep his back to a wall and see the entire space at once. He has begun to arrive late and leave early, missing opportunities to discuss custom orders, and his sales have slipped. His reputation for meticulous work has been compromised because he refuses to engage in the physical aspects of the craft, fearing that a sudden touch will trigger the memory. Ethan has been seeing a therapist for the past two months, hoping to untangle the web of triggers and memories that have taken over his life. He tells his therapist that he is most afraid of losing his job entirely and that he hopes to regain a sense of control over his heart and over the shop. The very fact that he is now willing to sit down with a professional indicates that he has come to recognize the destructive cycle he has lived in for years, even if he still struggles to break free from the loop.
